scenes.say: Add one item to the front of a million. An array shifts them all. A list re-points two links. By the end you'll reverse a list, find its middle, catch a cycle, with zero extra memory.
Today you will do three things. Insert and delete by re-pointing. Reverse a list in one pass. Then find a middle, catch a cycle, and merge.
lines: Reverse a list in one pass

scenes.title: Insert at the front
scenes.statement: Add a new value at the front of a sequence of a million items as cheaply as possible.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. A million items, and a new five goes first. An array shifts every item. A list re-points two links.

scenes.head: A treasure hunt
scenes.say: Think of a treasure hunt. The start card is the head: it says where clue one is. Each clue is a node: a prize, plus where the next clue is. That where is a pointer. The last clue says nowhere. To reach clue three, follow every clue before it.

scenes.head: Insert 5 at the head
scenes.say: Start with ten, twenty, thirty. Head points at ten. Now insert five at the front. First, make the new node. Second, point it at ten, the old first. Third, move head to the new node. Nothing shifted. Two assignments, so O of one.

arrows.cue: move head to the new node

changes.cue: move head to the new node

scenes.head: A node and insertHead
scenes.say: A node is a value and a pointer to the next node. The print helper follows pointers until null. Insert at the head: make the node, point it at the old first, move head.

steps.cue: point it at the old first

scenes.say: Your turn. Swap the last two steps. Move head first, then point the new node at head. What does the list look like?
scenes.q: Run `head = n;` before `n->next = head;`. What happens?

scenes.head: Order matters
scenes.say: Five pointing at five. Head moved first, so when the new node copies head, it copies itself. Walk the list: five, five, five, forever. And ten, twenty, thirty? Nothing points at them anymore. Lost, and leaked. Re-point the new node first, then move head.

scenes.head: Build a list, then print it
scenes.say: Build back to front. Insert thirty, then twenty, then ten, then five. Print follows the pointers from head: five, ten, twenty, thirty. An empty list is just head equal to null, and the same code works. That answers the problem: two links, not a million moves.

scenes.title: Delete a value
scenes.statement: Remove the node holding 20 from the list 5, 10, 20, 30.
scenes.say: Next problem. Delete twenty from five, ten, twenty, thirty. We should end with five, ten, thirty.

scenes.head: Delete 20
scenes.say: Walk to the node before it. That's ten. Call it p. Remember the doomed node, twenty, as dead. Point ten past it, straight at thirty. Twenty is cut out of the chain. Then delete it, or the memory leaks.

scenes.head: eraseAfter
scenes.say: Three lines. Remember the doomed node. Skip over it. Then free it. Run it, and ten now points to thirty. Finding p costs O of n if you don't hold it. The unlinking itself is O of one.
Your turn. A million nodes, and you hold a pointer to one in the middle. What does inserting right after it cost?
scenes.q: Insert right after a node you hold, in 1,000,000 nodes. Cost?

scenes.head: insertAfter
scenes.say: O of one. Only two pointers change, however long the list is. The new node takes over p's old next, then p points at the new node. From five, ten, thirty, put seven after ten.

scenes.head: List versus array
scenes.say: Compare. Reading item k: instant in an array, a long walk in a list. Inserting at the front: the array shifts everything, the list re-points. Memory: arrays are one cache friendly block. Nodes scatter, each with a pointer. A doubly linked list adds prev, so you can unlink a held node. C plus plus has both. In practice, vector usually wins. Delete solved: re-point around it.
rows: prev too: unlink a held node

scenes.title: Reverse a list
scenes.statement: Reverse a singly linked list in place.
scenes.say: The classic. Reverse one, two, three, four into four, three, two, one. Linear time, and no extra memory.

scenes.head: A line holding hands
scenes.say: Reversing a list is a favorite warm up. Picture four people in a line, each holding the next person's hand. Each one remembers who is next, lets go, and grabs the hand behind. Flip every hold, and the line runs the other way.

scenes.head: Reverse 1, 2, 3, 4
scenes.say: Reverse one, two, three, four. Prev starts at null, head at one. Save node two, so we don't lose it. Now flip: one points back at null. Slide prev and head forward. Two points back at one. Slide once more. Three points back at two. And slide. Four points back at three. Head runs off the end, so prev, at four, is the new front.

scenes.head: reverse in one pass
scenes.say: In code, four lines in a loop. Save next. Flip the pointer to prev. Move prev to head. Move head to the saved next. At null, return prev. One pass, O of n time, no extra memory.
Your turn. We forget to save next, and advance with head's next instead. What does print of prev show?
scenes.q: Skip saving next: `head = head->next;` after the flip. Prints?

scenes.head: The bug, run for real
scenes.say: Just one. After the flip, head's next is prev, which is null. So head becomes null, the loop ends, and nodes two, three and four are lost. Always save next before re-pointing. That solves reversing: save, flip, step.

panels.label: bug

scenes.title: Middle of a list
scenes.statement: Return the middle node of a singly linked list in a single pass.
scenes.say: Find the middle in one pass. Take one to five: the middle is three. No counting the length first.

scenes.head: Two runners
scenes.say: Two runners start together. Slow moves one step per tick. Fast moves two. When fast reaches the end, slow has covered half: the middle.

scenes.head: Middle of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
scenes.say: Take one to five. Slow and fast both start at the first node. Slow moves one, fast moves two. Step one: slow goes to two, fast goes to three. Step two: slow goes to three, fast goes to five. Fast can't go further, so stop. Slow is at the middle: node three.

scenes.head: middle
scenes.say: Both start at head. While fast and its next exist, slow steps once and fast twice. Check fast first, or you read null. Then slow is the middle: it prints three.
Your turn. Now six nodes, one to six. An even length has two middles. Which node does our loop return? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: List 1 to 6. What value does `middle` return?

scenes.head: Even length: the second middle
scenes.say: Four, the second of the two middle nodes. Both start at one. Slow to two, fast to three. Slow to three, fast to five. Slow to four, and fast steps off the end, to null. Even lengths give the second middle. That answers it: slow lands on the middle.

scenes.title: Does it loop?
scenes.statement: Tell whether a linked list contains a cycle.
scenes.say: Does this list loop forever? Five points back to two, so the answer is true. And we get no visited set.

scenes.head: Five points back to two
scenes.say: A bug that never crashes: the program just hangs. In this list, five points back to two. A plain walk never ends. Slow and fast both start at one. Round one: slow to two, fast to three. Round two: slow to three, fast jumps to five. Round three: slow to four, fast wraps around to three. Round four: slow to five, fast catches up. They meet.

scenes.head: hasCycle
scenes.say: Same loop as the middle, with one check. Slow steps once, fast twice. After each move, compare them. A match means a loop. If fast falls off the end, return false. Checking fast first avoids reading null.
Your turn. Three nodes, and three points back to one. Where do slow and fast first meet?
scenes.q: Nodes 1, 2, 3; node 3 points to 1. Where do slow and fast meet?

scenes.head: A loop of three
scenes.say: Node one, after three rounds. Round one: slow to two, fast to three. Round two: slow to three, fast wraps around to two. Round three: slow wraps to one, and fast, taking two steps, lands on one too. They meet.

scenes.head: Where does the loop start?
scenes.say: Where does the loop start? Slow and fast both sit at five. Send fast home, to node one. Both step one at a time now. Slow goes round to two. Fast goes to two. They meet at two, and that is the start of the loop. That answers it: yes, and where.

scenes.title: Merge two sorted lists
scenes.statement: Merge two sorted lists into one sorted list by relinking the nodes.
scenes.say: Last problem. Merge one, three, five with two, four. We want one through five, by relinking nodes.

scenes.head: A zipper with a fake first tooth
scenes.say: Merging sorted lists works like a zipper: always take the smaller front. One problem: which node becomes the head? You can't know until you compare. The fix is a dummy head, a fake node placed first. Build behind it, return its next.

scenes.head: Merge 1, 3, 5 and 2, 4
scenes.say: Merge one, three, five with two, four. Start with a dummy head, a fake node that holds the place. Compare one and two. One wins, so it's linked after dummy. Compare three and two. Two wins. Compare three and four. Three wins. Compare five and four. Four wins. List b is empty, so link the rest, five, on the end.

scenes.head: mergeLists
scenes.say: Make the dummy, and let tail point at it. While both lists have nodes, link the smaller front after tail and advance that list. Then move tail. When one runs out, link the rest of the other. Return dummy's next.
Your turn. Merge one, two, three with seven, eight. When the loop ends, what is left to link on the end?
scenes.q: Merge 1,2,3 with 7,8. After the loop, what's still unlinked?

scenes.head: The leftover tail
scenes.say: Seven, eight. List a ran out after three, so list b is untouched. One link finishes the job: tail's next points at seven, and eight comes along. No copying, no second loop. That's our merge: relink, never copy.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: How does a list work? Nodes with next pointers, head marks the first. Versus an array? Front insert O of one, reading item k O of n. Why not always a list? No index, poor cache, so vector wins. Common mistake? Moving head before saving the old first.
rows: nodes: value + next pointer; head points at first
front insert O(1), read item k O(n)
no index, poor cache: vector usually wins
moving head before saving the old first

scenes.say: Self test. Slow and fast just met inside a loop. How do you find where the loop starts?
scenes.q: Slow and fast met in a cycle. How do you find the start?
scenes.answer: reset one to head, step both by 1

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: How do you reverse? Three pointers, O of n time, O of one space. Find the middle? Slow takes one step, fast two. Slow ends at the middle. Why do they meet? Fast gains a step per round. Where does the cycle start? Reset one pointer to head, step both by one.
rows: prev, current, next: O(n) time, O(1) space
slow 1 step, fast 2: slow ends at middle
fast gains a step per round: gap closes
reset one to head, step both by one

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Why a dummy head? No special case for the first node or an empty list. How do you merge? Link the smaller front behind tail, attach the rest. Common mistake? Not saving next before re-pointing, or reading fast next without checking fast.
rows: no special case for first node or empty list
link smaller front behind tail, attach the rest

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Solve these next. LeetCode two oh six, reverse linked list, is today's reverse loop. LeetCode twenty one, merge two sorted lists, is the dummy head. LeetCode one forty two, linked list cycle two, finds where the loop starts.
So say this. Re-point in the right order. Reverse by saving next, flipping, stepping. Slow and fast find middles and cycles. A dummy head cleans up merging.
lines: Node = value + next. Re-point in the right order.
Reverse: save next, flip, step. O(1) memory.
Slow/fast: middle, cycles. Dummy head: merging.
